job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Dana Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my mum and dad in Eldermoor, in my old bedroom, which at 23 is not where I thought I'd be. Mornings I help my mum with the church flower rota or the garden, then I do my applications at the kitchen table. In the afternoons I walk to the post office and check the notice board at the farm co-op, because local firms still put adverts there. I studied accounting at Whitcombe College and finished top of the class, with a summer at the co-op's bookkeeping office and another at a county accountancy practice. Five months on, I've had nine interviews, no offer, and 35,000 of student debt that my parents can't help with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I expected. People always get carried away with new gadgets, and the real work stays the same. I'd tell people at church that honest work still counts and that we shouldn't be afraid of machines that don't do much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still hard. I have 35,000 to pay off, no savings to speak of and very few firms within reach of Eldermoor. A plateau means the world stays as it is, and as it is there is no place for me yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to every interview, even when it's a long bus ride. I'd ask my pastor and the co-op manager whether they know anyone who needs a bookkeeper, since local trust gets people hired more than online forms do. I'd also say yes to a part-time role at the co-op, even if it's below my qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Patient on the outside and worried underneath. I pray about it, and I try not to take the worry to bed with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of those nine interviews came closest, and why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The county practice, because they said I was the best candidate on paper but hired a man with two years of experience. The partner told me kindly that it came down to who could start without training. That's the story of every interview: experience, experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you make of the debt, looking back on the choice to go to college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't regret the degree, but I think the college oversold it. They told us that a degree would be the ticket, and the loans came easily, and nobody mentioned the entry-level squeeze. I'd rather young people learned a trade with an employer paying them while they learn.

say: Honest work still counts, and we shouldn't fear machines that don't do much **at all**.
People get carried away with new **gadgets**.
think: A plateau means the world stays as it is, and there's no **place** for me yet.
I owe **35,000** with no savings and few firms near Eldermoor.
do: Go to every **interview**, however long the bus ride.
Ask my pastor and the co-op manager who needs a **bookkeeper**.
Say yes to a part-time role at the **co-op**, even below my qualification.
feel: **Patient** outside and worried underneath, with prayer to help.

fieldNote: Blames **colleges** and easy loans more than firms or machines.
Prefers local trust and church **contacts** to online forms.
Would take a below-level **co-op** role rather than stay idle.

steps.text: Go to every interview, including the long bus rides
Ask the pastor and the co-op manager who needs a bookkeeper
Take a part-time co-op bookkeeping job
Send three local applications each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we shouldn't rush to trust it, and I'd say it quietly at church. The tools can do the sums but they can't be held to account, and I'd want a person to sign. I'd tell people to keep their own skills sharp so they don't depend on a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm scared. Everything I did at the co-op, the invoices, the payroll, the monthly checks, is what the programs do now. Small offices like the co-op may just buy the software, and then the bookkeeper's seat goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself try it, though it goes against my grain. I'd ask the co-op manager whether I could learn their software on a trial basis. And I'd keep looking at jobs that need a person in the room, like helping the older farmers with their tax and subsidy forms. They don't trust a screen and they'd pay for someone they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried and a bit insulted, if I'm honest. I worked for this degree and I don't want to be the last of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. What worries you about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want to depend on something I can't question. If it makes a mistake and I sign it, my name is on the error. At the co-op I had to explain every figure to the board, and a machine can't stand up and do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs do you think survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones with a person on the other side of the table. A farmer who's frightened about a tax bill wants a face and a handshake. I think that part of accounting survives, and it's the part I'd like to be good at.

say: We shouldn't rush to trust it, because the tools can't be held to **account**.
think: Everything I did at the co-op, the invoices and payroll, is what the **programs** do now.
A small office may buy the software and the **bookkeeper's seat** goes.

Ask the co-op manager for a **trial** on their software.
Offer tax and subsidy form help to older **farmers**.
feel: **Worried** and a bit insulted: I don't want to be the last of something.

fieldNote: Resists the tools on **accountability**, not on a fear of the new.
Her fix is **local**: trusted contacts and older farmers.

steps.text: Ask the co-op manager for a trial on their accounting software
Offer tax and subsidy form help to older farmers for a fee
Apply for jobs where clients meet a person across the desk

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not right and nobody can be expected to be ready. I'd say that the government and the big firms have a duty to the people who'll lose out, but I'd also say families need to hold together. I'd be speaking mostly at church and with neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be frightened. Everything I trained for is on the list of things that disappear first, and two years isn't long enough to learn something else. I don't think I'd get a full accounting job and I'd have 35,000 to pay off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at whatever I could get close to home, like helping at the co-op, a shop or the post office. I'd learn a practical trade if there's an apprenticeship, since robots for hands-on work come three years later, and I could learn a skill that way. I'd also stay at home and put everything I earn at the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened but resolved. I'd try not to let the fear take over my days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that I can stay in my room, pay board when I can and keep my faith. And that we'd manage it together, as families always have. I'd also be honest that it would be hard on them, because I'd be at home for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you draw the line on asking for public help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't want a handout, but I'd accept help that's linked to work, like an apprenticeship scheme or a loan pause with conditions. I'd take it if my family needed it, because not eating is worse than pride.

say: Nobody can be expected to be **ready**, and big firms owe something to those who lose out.
think: Everything I trained for is on the list of what disappears **first**.
Two years isn't enough to learn something **else**, and I'd still owe 35,000.

fieldNote: Won't ask for **handouts** but accepts help tied to work, in line with her outlook.
Looks to family and **church** as the first safety net.
Understands the three-year hands-on **gap** and uses it.

steps.text: Apply for a practical trade apprenticeship in the county
Ask my parents to let me stay home and pay board when I can
Put every wage at the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a warning, and sensible people should use it. I'd tell the young people at church to learn a trade or something where you meet the customer. I wouldn't tell people to be afraid, because fear helps nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I can do something with it. If I got a job at the co-op or a county firm in the next year, I'd have three or four years of experience, and I could shift into advice work before the main change. The debt is the part I can't shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first accounting job even if it's modest, and learn the software they use. I'd put a third of every wage at the loan, and I'd study for the next level of my accounting qualification in the evenings. I'd keep up the church network, because it brings me introductions that no form does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit steadier than the two year one. Five years lets me hope, and I need to hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd say the same as my mum: keep your head down, work hard, pray, and don't borrow more. They'd also be good for introductions, and one or two of them run firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What advice would your church friends give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say pay off the debt first, because it's the one thing that doesn't change, and keep the family close. Whatever happens, I'd rather be someone who stayed steady.

The **debt** is the part I can't shift.

fieldNote: Time gives her **hope** and a plan with the church as her network.

steps.text: Take a first accounting job and learn the firm's software
Put a third of every wage at the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that ten years is generous, and we should use it by teaching people skills that last. I'd say it at church and to the college. I wouldn't spend time worrying aloud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fairly secure. I could get a job, qualify, pay off the debt and still have years in which to learn something new. It's the one where I think my plans have room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first accounting job, then spend three years qualifying. I'd clear the debt in about seven years and save for a house in Eldermoor. I'd also try the AI tools gradually, because by then they'd be normal and I'd have to stop avoiding them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I wouldn't say relaxed, because I'm not made that way, but I'd sleep properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you marry and settle where you are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope so, yes. I'd like to marry in my late twenties and settle near my parents, because I don't want to leave Eldermoor. Ten years means I can build that without pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger people at church about careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn something that lets them work with people, and to save early. Keep your faith and your family, and be useful to the people around you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one. It leaves no time for a person like me, who needs to see a plan. If it happened, what would help is work that comes with training, a loan pause with fair conditions and employers who'd give a local girl a first chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that we're not ungrateful. Our parents sacrificed to send us and we worked hard. We'd like to be able to repay that with honest work, not with a story about how things went wrong.

headlineQuote: We're not ungrateful. Our parents sacrificed to send us and we worked hard.
portrait: Dana is 23, top of her accounting class, living in her old bedroom in **Eldermoor** with 35,000 of debt.
She is traditional, churchgoing and wary of handouts, preferring work, apprenticeships and family support.
She has never used AI tools and resists them on **accountability** grounds, which leaves her exposed.
She finds her strongest fallback in local trust: the pastor, the co-op and older farmers.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, because she can't plan, retrain and clear her debt in two years.
whatWouldHelp: Work that comes with **training**, a loan pause with fair conditions and local employers giving her a first chance.
